threat: Steal Automotive Intellectual Property from Design and R&D Systems
threat_description: Adversaries target the engineering networks, design repositories, and simulation platforms where automotive OEMs invest billions developing next-generation vehicle architectures, powertrain technologies, and safety systems. Vehicle design blueprints, crash simulation results, battery chemistry data, and ADAS algorithms represent years of competitive advantage compressed into accessible digital files. State-sponsored groups and well-funded competitors have demonstrated they will conduct sustained intrusion campaigns against these environments — the data they extract can replicate an OEM's R&D program at a fraction of the cost. The attacker does not need to build a vehicle. They need to breach the network that designed one.

motives.motive: Acquire proprietary vehicle design data and engineering specifications to replicate OEM technology without R&D investment

components.name: Design and Engineering Systems
components.description: CAD platforms, PLM systems, and simulation environments storing vehicle design blueprints, crash test models, and engineering specifications — Siemens Teamcenter, PTC Windchill, Dassault CATIA. The highest-concentration repository of automotive IP in the OEM ecosystem.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Weak password policies on engineering platform accounts let adversaries take over an engineer's identity through credential stuffing, password spraying or targeted phishing, and the platform has no compensating control that would distinguish the resulting session from a legitimate one — a single recovered password yields the complete vehicle architecture developed under that account.

Authorization is not enforced on design-repository reads: any authenticated user with engineering network access can request vehicle blueprints outside their assigned programs, and resource identifiers in engineering platform URLs and access tokens can be manipulated to enumerate design files belonging to other vehicle programs.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-1220: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Access control on the design archive is all-or-nothing rather than scoped: there is no separation between read access to a current project and read access to the full historical design archive, and externally facing partner and contractor portals inherit the same coarse grant, surfacing far more design data than any single engagement requires.

components.name: Research and Development Networks
components.description: Segmented R&D networks hosting emerging technology research — battery innovation, autonomous driving algorithms, next-generation powertrain data. These networks hold pre-competitive IP that has not yet entered the formal design pipeline.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: SSRF vulnerabilities in R&D collaboration platforms allow attackers to manipulate internal server requests and pivot from internet-facing portals to isolated research repositories holding pre-competitive automotive technology data.

Security-relevant access events on R&D data stores are not recorded, so adversaries conducting long-dwell IP exfiltration campaigns leave no reconstructable trail — technology roadmaps and research findings are extracted over months before any anomaly surfaces, and the omission also prevents scoping the loss after the fact.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-311: Missing Encryption of Sensitive Data
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Automotive design blueprints and R&D data stored or transmitted without encryption can be intercepted during transfer between engineering sites or exfiltrated from storage — unencrypted IP is immediately usable by any party who acquires it.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: SQL injection vulnerabilities in R&D data management databases allow attackers to bypass application-layer access controls and extract the full design archive — vehicle program history, simulation results, and engineering specifications — through the application's own database connection.

motives.motive: Destroy or corrupt automotive design data to sabotage a competitor's vehicle development program

components.name: Design and Engineering Systems
components.description: CAD platforms and simulation environments where vehicle designs are authored and validated. Destruction of design data eliminates the accumulated work of vehicle programs that took years to develop.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Improper input validation in design management interfaces allows attackers to inject malicious payloads that corrupt simulation models and overwrite engineering specifications — a corrupted crash simulation result that passes undetected introduces safety defects into the production vehicle program.

Deserialization vulnerabilities in engineering data exchange pipelines allow attackers to inject manipulated design objects that corrupt vehicle blueprints or introduce hidden defects into simulation models shared across engineering teams.

threat: Corrupt Automotive Manufacturing to Produce Defective Vehicles
threat_description: Adversaries target automated manufacturing and production control systems to manipulate assembly parameters, corrupt production schedules, or introduce fabrication defects that persist into finished vehicles. Modern automotive manufacturing is fully automated — robots execute thousands of precise operations per vehicle based entirely on software instructions. An attacker who modifies those instructions does not need physical access to the production line. Defects introduced here propagate silently across every vehicle produced until the manipulation is detected — which may not happen until vehicles are in the hands of consumers and warranty claims or safety incidents expose the sabotage.

motives.motive: Introduce manufacturing defects into vehicle production to trigger costly recalls and damage brand reputation

components.name: Automated Manufacturing and Production Control Systems
components.description: PLC-driven robotic assembly systems, production scheduling platforms, and quality control automation managing vehicle fabrication — Siemens SIMATIC, Rockwell Automation FactoryTalk, ABB robotic controllers. Every vehicle assembly parameter is controlled by software these systems execute.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-15: External Control of System or Configuration Setting
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Assembly parameters that the production line treats as trusted configuration — torque targets, weld dwell times, material specifications, inspection tolerances — are settable from interfaces that do not establish who may change them or bound what a plausible value is, so an attacker or a mis-scoped operator can drive systematic fabrication defects into every vehicle on the line by writing values the controllers accept without challenge.

Deserialization vulnerabilities in production management platforms allow attackers to inject manipulated assembly sequences — silently altering the physical operations performed on vehicles in ways that introduce structural or safety defects that survive quality inspection.

Authorization is not enforced on production-control write operations: any attacker with a manufacturing network foothold, and any operator acting outside their role, can modify assembly torque specifications, weld dwell times, production tolerances and inspection acceptance criteria — the changes propagate to every robot and quality gate on the line without physical presence and without a second approval.

components.name: Industrial Control Systems (ICS) and Smart Manufacturing Platforms
components.description: SCADA systems and ICS infrastructure managing factory-wide automation, robotics coordination, and safety system monitoring — Honeywell Experion, Emerson DeltaV, Schneider Electric EcoStruxure. These platforms orchestrate the physical manufacturing environment.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Weak password policies on ICS management accounts give attackers authenticated access to the SCADA systems controlling factory-wide automation — one recovered credential is enough to modify robot programs and disable safety interlocks across the facility.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Safety- and production-critical ICS functions are reachable without any authentication step: legacy SCADA and PLC management interfaces expose engineering-workstation and controller functions to anyone on the manufacturing network, because the protocols predate identity controls and cannot enforce them.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection')
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Code injection vulnerabilities in smart manufacturing management software allow attackers to introduce malicious scripts that alter machine operating parameters or disable quality control gates, enabling systematic defect introduction across production batches.

threat: Lock Down Automotive Operations for Ransom
threat_description: Adversaries deploy ransomware across OEM production infrastructure, dealer management SaaS platforms, and supplier networks — encrypting the operational systems that keep vehicles moving through manufacturing and into consumer hands. Automotive manufacturing runs on just-in-time principles: a production line that cannot access its scheduling system or PLC configurations stops generating revenue from the moment of encryption. Ransomware attacks on the automotive sector more than doubled in 2025, accounting for 44% of all incidents — the JLR attack alone halted production for several weeks and required government loan guarantees to stabilise its supply chain. The math is simple: shutting down automotive production is expensive, which makes it an ideal extortion target.

motives.motive: Encrypt OEM production systems to halt vehicle manufacturing and extort ransom payment under sustained operational pressure

components.name: OEM Enterprise IT and Production Systems
components.description: Enterprise IT infrastructure and production control systems operated by automotive OEMs — the interdependency between corporate IT and manufacturing OT means ransomware that enters through IT quickly reaches production scheduling and line control systems.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Weak credential policies let ransomware operators obtain a working OEM enterprise account through phishing or credential stuffing, and the absence of MFA on VPN and remote desktop access means that single credential is also the lateral-movement authority used to reach production scheduling and line control.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Absence of integrity verification on software updates and third-party components allows ransomware payloads to be introduced through the OEM's own update mechanisms — trusted software distribution channels become the delivery path for production-encrypting malware.

Security-relevant events across OEM production and IT systems are not recorded, so ransomware operator dwell activity leaves no trail — attackers spend weeks mapping systems, disabling backups and staging encryption targets, and the omission prevents both detection during that window and scoping of the blast radius afterwards.

components.name: Dealer Management SaaS Provider Platform
components.description: Cloud-hosted dealer management platforms serving thousands of dealerships from shared infrastructure — CDK Global, Reynolds and Reynolds, Dealertrack. A single platform-level compromise simultaneously locks out every subscribing dealership with no per-property recovery path.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Authorization is not enforced on dealer SaaS platform administrative functions: a single compromised platform credential can act across every subscribing dealership's environment rather than only its own, so one account takeover deploys encryption payloads to all customers simultaneously.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-829: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Compromise of a dealer SaaS platform's software update pipeline allows ransomware operators to distribute malicious payloads through the platform's own trusted update mechanism to all connected dealership environments.

motives.motive: Compromise a supplier to propagate ransomware into connected OEM networks and amplify disruption across the supply chain

components.name: Automotive Supplier Network Integration
components.description: Interconnected supplier systems providing components, software, and services to automotive manufacturers — trusted network connections between suppliers and OEMs create lateral movement paths that bypass OEM perimeter controls.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Weak authentication on supplier-to-OEM network integration points allows ransomware groups to compromise a small supplier and propagate encryption payloads into connected manufacturer networks — exploiting the just-in-time supply chain dependency to halt OEM production without ever directly attacking the OEM perimeter.

Supplier connections into OEM networks are authorized at network level rather than per integration function, so ransomware operators who compromise a supplier can reach OEM production systems through an established trusted path — the weaker supplier's security posture becomes the effective authorization boundary for an OEM-scale disruption.

threat: Compromise Vehicle Firmware and Safety-Critical Software
threat_description: Adversaries target vehicle ECU firmware, embedded safety software, and OTA update infrastructure to introduce malicious modifications that compromise vehicle safety systems, enable remote control, or create hidden vulnerabilities exploitable at scale. Modern vehicles contain over 100 ECUs running hundreds of millions of lines of code — a single compromised update pushed to millions of vehicles simultaneously represents a safety incident of unprecedented scale. The attack surface spans the entire firmware lifecycle: supplier development environments, OEM integration pipelines, OTA distribution infrastructure, and the vehicles themselves. The attacker does not need physical access to any vehicle — they need access to the software that runs in all of them.

motives.motive: Inject malicious firmware into vehicle ECUs to enable remote control or disable safety systems across a vehicle fleet

components.name: Vehicle Software and Embedded Firmware Systems
components.description: ECU firmware repositories, vehicle software build systems, and embedded control software managing braking, steering, engine, and safety functions — Vector CANdb++, AUTOSAR toolchains, OEM-proprietary firmware development environments.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Hard-coded credentials in vehicle firmware update tools or ECU programming interfaces cannot be revoked — any attacker who discovers them gains permanent, unrevokable ability to authenticate to firmware update workflows and push malicious ECU software to any vehicle using that toolchain.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: The ECU firmware update authorization chain has no authentication step on its critical function: update packages accepted by the vehicle are not tied to a verified OEM identity, so anyone who can reach the update interface can push firmware to safety-critical ECUs fleet-wide.

sub_components.name: ECU firmware build and distribution pipeline

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Vehicle firmware update mechanisms that do not verify cryptographic signatures allow attackers to substitute legitimate updates with malicious firmware — the vehicle accepts the modified firmware as authentic and applies it to safety-critical ECUs.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-319: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Cleartext transmission of firmware update packages exposes vehicle software to interception and modification in transit — an attacker who can intercept the update channel can modify firmware before it reaches the vehicle without triggering signature validation.

components.name: Remote Vehicle Maintenance and OTA Update Systems
components.description: Over-the-air update infrastructure distributing firmware to deployed vehicle fleets — OEM OTA platforms, telematics-based update delivery, and remote diagnostic systems. A single OTA infrastructure compromise scales firmware attacks to every connected vehicle simultaneously.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Authorization is not enforced on OTA distribution functions: unauthorized firmware packages can be injected into the update pipeline, and vehicle targeting parameters — model, region, fleet operator — can be altered to direct a malicious build at a chosen population. The distribution system then delivers it to the connected fleet as a legitimate OEM update.

motives.motive: Compromise supplier-embedded firmware before vehicles are manufactured to introduce safety vulnerabilities at scale

components.name: Supplier-Embedded Software and Firmware Systems
components.description: Firmware development and distribution infrastructure at Tier 1 and Tier 2 automotive suppliers — component ECU software, sensor firmware, and telematics unit software integrated into vehicles before OEM assembly. Supplier compromise introduces vulnerabilities into every vehicle model using that component.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Malicious code introduced into supplier firmware development environments is compiled into component firmware and shipped to OEM assembly lines — every vehicle incorporating the compromised component carries the embedded vulnerability into production without OEM-level inspection of supplier binary deliverables.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Supplier firmware distribution chains that do not enforce cryptographic integrity verification allow substitution of legitimate firmware with backdoored versions — OEMs that do not independently verify supplier binary deliverables have no mechanism to detect the substitution before vehicle assembly.

Weak password policies on supplier firmware repositories allow attackers to compromise developer accounts and introduce malicious code into component firmware before it is distributed to OEM assembly lines — the attack scales to every vehicle model incorporating the affected component.

threat: Manipulate Vehicle Software to Defeat Emissions and Safety Standards
threat_description: Adversaries modify vehicle ECU software controlling engine management, emissions systems, and safety calibration to defeat regulatory compliance requirements — altering performance parameters to exceed emissions limits, disable mandatory safety features, or enable configurations that fail type approval. This threat encompasses both organized defeat device fraud — where vehicles are deliberately tuned to circumvent emissions testing — and targeted attacks by competitors or hostile actors to create regulatory liability for OEMs. A vehicle software platform that can be modified to pass emissions testing in one mode and disable those controls in normal operation is both a compliance failure and a security vulnerability.

motives.motive: Modify vehicle ECU calibrations to defeat emissions controls and generate fraudulent regulatory compliance

components.name: Vehicle ECU Calibration and Engine Control Systems
components.description: Engine control units and emissions management software governing fuel injection, exhaust after-treatment, and emissions monitoring systems — Bosch EDC/MED controllers, Continental PCM platforms. These systems determine whether a vehicle complies with regional emissions regulations.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Authorization is not enforced on ECU calibration writes: emissions and safety calibration parameters can be modified without OEM approval, because the programming interface checks only that a tool is connected and not whether the party operating it is permitted to change the software that determines regulatory compliance.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-15: External Control of System or Configuration Setting
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Emissions- and safety-relevant calibration values — fuel maps, torque limits, after-treatment dosing thresholds — are accepted by the ECU as externally supplied configuration without a plausibility or provenance check, so tuning software can write a map that defeats regulatory controls and the ECU applies it as though it were an OEM calibration.

components.name: Vehicle Diagnostic and Tuning Systems
components.description: OBD-connected diagnostic and tuning platforms used by dealerships, aftermarket tuners, and service centers — VCDS, HP Tuners, OEM dealer programming tools. These systems provide direct write access to ECU calibration parameters.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Authorization is not enforced on diagnostic-tool ECU write functions: parties can reach calibration write operations beyond their permitted scope, so unlicensed tuning software and any party with physical OBD access can apply emissions-defeat modifications that are indistinguishable from legitimate dealer calibration updates.

threat: Harvest Driver Location and Telemetry Data from Connected Vehicle Platforms
threat_description: Adversaries target the cloud platforms, telematics backends, and EV charging networks that continuously collect driver location, journey patterns, speed profiles, and behavioral data from connected vehicles. Modern vehicles are surveillance platforms on wheels — they generate more personal data per hour than most consumer devices, transmitted continuously to OEM cloud infrastructure with minimal user control or transparency. A telematics platform breach that exposed 2.7 million vehicle owners' records — including Social Security numbers — in early 2025 demonstrated the scale of harm possible. The attacker does not need to touch the vehicle. They need to breach the cloud that receives everything the vehicle reports.

motives.motive: Extract continuous driver location histories and behavioral profiles for surveillance, stalking, or targeted exploitation

components.name: Vehicle Telematics Platform
components.description: Cloud platforms collecting and storing real-time vehicle location, speed, acceleration, and driver behavior data from connected vehicle fleets — OEM telematics backends, Verizon Connect, Geotab, Samsara. These platforms hold continuous location histories for millions of vehicles.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Authorization on telematics cloud APIs is not bound to vehicle ownership: user-controlled vehicle identifiers in API requests can be iterated to retrieve telemetry belonging to other owners, and any valid platform credential reaches journey histories across the fleet.

Telematics API credentials are inadequately protected at both ends: endpoint authentication is weak enough to enumerate vehicle telemetry records, and API keys embedded in connected-vehicle mobile applications can be recovered by reverse engineering, giving an attacker authenticated access to continuous location data for every vehicle in the compromised credential's scope.

components.name: EV Charging Network Platform
components.description: Cloud-based platforms managing EV charging sessions and collecting driver identity, payment credentials, vehicle identifiers, and charging location data — ChargePoint, IONITY, Electrify America backends. Charging records create a precise location history tied to driver identity.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-311: Missing Encryption of Sensitive Data
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Unencrypted storage of EV charging session records exposes driver identity, payment credentials, vehicle identification numbers, and charging location histories — charging session records concentrate identity, payment and location data in a single store.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: SQL injection in EV charging network databases allows bulk extraction of driver identity records, payment credentials, and charging location histories — the centralized nature of charging platform databases means a single injection point yields data for the entire registered driver population.

threat: Gain Unauthorized Remote Control of Connected Vehicles
threat_description: Adversaries exploit broken authorization in connected vehicle APIs, compromised aftermarket accessories, and OBD-connected devices to issue unauthorized remote commands — unlocking doors, starting engines, tracking location, or manipulating vehicle functions — against vehicles they do not own. Ransomware attacks on vehicles themselves emerged in 2025, with attackers remotely immobilizing individual vehicles for targeted extortion. Connected vehicle APIs that serve legitimate functions like remote start and stolen vehicle recovery become the attacker's control interface when authorization fails. The attacker does not need to break into the vehicle. They need to break into the API that controls it.

motives.motive: Take control of connected-vehicle command APIs to unlock, start and locate vehicles for theft and resale

components.name: Connected Vehicle API Gateway
components.description: API infrastructure enabling remote vehicle command and control — OEM connected vehicle APIs, third-party mobility platform integrations, vehicle remote start and stolen vehicle recovery systems. Every legitimate remote function is also an unauthorized access vector when authorization fails.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: The connected-vehicle command API authorizes on credential validity rather than vehicle ownership: user-controlled vehicle identifiers can be iterated to issue door unlock, engine start and location tracking commands against vehicles belonging to other owners, and no server-side check ties the caller to the target vehicle.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-1220: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: API authorization is too coarse to separate the operations a caller may perform: a single credential scope covers read telemetry, remote command and account management alike, so any token that reaches the gateway carries fleet-scale remote-control authority rather than the narrow permission the calling feature actually needs.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Absence of rate limiting on connected vehicle API authentication endpoints allows automated credential stuffing against vehicle owner accounts — systematically compromising accounts to gain authorized access to remote vehicle control functions at fleet scale.

motives.motive: Establish persistent covert access to an individual's vehicle through a compromised aftermarket accessory for stalking or targeted extortion

components.name: Aftermarket Vehicle Accessories and OBD Interface
components.description: Third-party telematics dongles, fleet tracking devices, and diagnostic accessories connected to the vehicle OBD port — devices that ship with hard-coded credentials and accept unsigned firmware, creating persistent bidirectional access to vehicle networks.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Aftermarket OBD accessories shipped with hard-coded default credentials that cannot be changed allow attackers who discover these credentials to gain remote access to any vehicle where the device is installed — a single credential discovery scales to the entire installed base of that device model.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: OBD accessories that accept unsigned firmware updates allow attackers to replace legitimate firmware with malicious versions that establish persistent CAN bus access — turning a fleet tracking dongle into a permanent vehicle network backdoor across every vehicle where it is installed.

sub_components.name: OBD port and CAN bus access scope

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Authorization is not enforced on vehicle OBD interface protocols: a compromised aftermarket device can issue ECU and CAN bus messages far beyond its intended diagnostic scope, because the vehicle authorizes by physical port presence rather than by the accessory's function, letting a telematics dongle command safety-relevant systems.

threat: Compromise Autonomous Vehicle Perception and Driving Decision Systems
threat_description: Adversaries target the AI perception models, sensor fusion pipelines, and driving decision systems of autonomous and semi-autonomous vehicles — introducing manipulated training data, backdoored models, or adversarial sensor inputs that cause vehicles to misidentify obstacles, ignore traffic controls, or make unsafe navigation decisions. Unlike traditional vehicle safety failures, AI perception attacks can be triggered on demand by anyone who knows the trigger, affect every vehicle running the compromised model simultaneously, and produce failures that appear statistically normal until the pattern is recognized. The attacker does not cause an accident — they cause the vehicle to cause one.

motives.motive: Introduce perception failures into autonomous driving AI to create unsafe vehicle behavior at scale

components.name: Autonomous Driving AI System
components.description: Machine learning models responsible for vehicle perception, object detection, path planning, and driving decisions — Mobileye EyeQ, Tesla FSD neural networks, Waymo perception stack. These models determine what the vehicle believes it sees and what it decides to do.

sub_components.name: On-vehicle AI model delivery and integrity

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: AI model artifacts are deployed to vehicles without cryptographic integrity or provenance verification, so a poisoned or backdoored perception model delivered over the OTA channel is accepted as authentic — the vehicle has no mechanism to distinguish a genuine OEM model update from an adversarially modified one, and begins making driving decisions on attacker-controlled perception logic.

Malicious code embedded in autonomous driving AI model artifacts during supply chain compromise introduces trigger-activated perception failures — the model behaves normally on standard inputs but produces dangerous misclassifications when specific trigger patterns appear in the vehicle's sensor environment.

Authorization is not enforced on autonomous-driving model management functions: parties able to reach the model registry can alter perception model parameters and promote a build to the fleet, changing how the vehicle classifies pedestrians, obstacles and traffic controls across every deployed vehicle.

components.name: ADAS Sensor and Perception Systems
components.description: LiDAR, radar, and camera sensor infrastructure providing environmental data to vehicle AI systems — Velodyne LiDAR, Continental radar, Mobileye camera perception. Sensor data integrity is the foundation on which all autonomous driving decisions rest.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-1039: Inadequate Detection or Handling of Adversarial Input Perturbations in Automated Recognition Mechanism
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: ADAS perception classifiers are trained on nominal driving environments and neither validate nor reject adversarial sensor input: LiDAR spoofing returns, projected or printed patterns on road surfaces and radar jamming are accepted as authoritative measurements. Physical perturbations imperceptible to a human observer cause systematic misclassification of obstacles, lane markings and traffic controls, and the vehicle acts on the result with full confidence.

threat: Disrupt Fleet Dispatch and EV Charging Operations
threat_description: Adversaries target fleet management platforms and EV charging network infrastructure to deny mobility services — rendering commercial vehicle fleets unable to dispatch, route, or maintain vehicles, and disabling EV charging availability across networks that drivers depend on. Fleet operators with no dispatch system cannot route vehicles, assign drivers, or confirm deliveries. EV charging networks taken offline strand drivers mid-journey and undermine confidence in electric mobility infrastructure. Both targets are centralized platforms: a single availability attack against the management platform simultaneously denies service to every operator or driver that depends on it.

motives.motive: Deny dispatch and routing capabilities to commercial fleet operators by disabling fleet management infrastructure

components.name: Fleet Management Platform
components.description: Cloud-based platforms managing vehicle dispatch, route optimization, driver assignment, and maintenance scheduling for commercial vehicle fleets — Samsara, Geotab, Verizon Connect, Fleetio. Fleet unavailability halts every logistics, delivery, and service operation the fleet supports.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Uncontrolled resource consumption in fleet management APIs allows request flooding to exhaust processing capacity — a sustained API flood denies dispatch and routing functions to all fleet operators simultaneously, bringing commercial delivery and logistics operations to a halt.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Fleet management platform updates distributed without integrity verification allow deployment of destructive payloads through the platform's own update mechanism — simultaneously corrupting dispatch and routing data for all connected fleet operators.

Weak authentication on fleet management administrative interfaces allows attackers to gain unauthorized access and disable or corrupt dispatch functions — a single compromised administrator account provides the ability to delete route assignments and driver schedules across all managed fleets.

motives.motive: Disable EV charging availability across networks to deny electric vehicle mobility and undermine EV adoption

components.name: EV Charging Network Platform
components.description: Cloud management infrastructure controlling charge point operations, session authentication, and energy management across EV charging networks — ChargePoint, IONITY, BP Pulse, Electrify America backends. Network-level disruption simultaneously disables all connected charge points.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Weak authentication on EV charging network management interfaces allows unauthorized parties to remotely manipulate charging session parameters, disable charge points, or interfere with energy demand management — disrupting charging availability for large numbers of EV drivers simultaneously.

Authorization is not enforced on EV charging network management functions: a party who reaches the management platform can remotely disable charge points across entire networks and alter energy demand management, because the platform authorizes at network scope rather than per charge point or per operator.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Absence of firmware integrity verification on EV charge point hardware allows push of malicious firmware updates that disable charging functionality or corrupt OCPP communication — a single malicious firmware broadcast can simultaneously brick charge points across an entire charging network.

threat: Expose Dealership Customer Records and Financial Data
threat_description: Adversaries target dealer management systems, customer financing platforms, and payment infrastructure to exfiltrate the comprehensive personal and financial data that automotive dealerships maintain on every customer — purchase history, financing applications, credit scores, payment card data, and government-issued identification. Dealerships are high-value targets: they hold credit application data equivalent to financial institutions, payment card data equivalent to retailers, and personal identification data equivalent to government systems — all in a single DMS platform. The 700Credit breach and OEM-level compromises in 2025 exposed dealer and consumer data across multiple brands simultaneously. A single DMS platform breach reaches every customer record that platform has ever processed.

motives.motive: Extract customer personal and financial records from dealer management systems for identity theft and fraud

components.name: Dealer Management System (DMS)
components.description: Comprehensive dealership operations platforms managing sales, service, financing, and customer relationships — CDK Global, Reynolds and Reynolds, Dealertrack, AutoSoft. These systems hold the complete personal and financial history of every customer who has ever transacted with the dealership.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Weak authentication on DMS administrative interfaces allows attackers to bypass identity verification and access comprehensive customer records — vehicle purchase history, financing data, and personal identification — for every customer the dealership has served.

Authorization on multi-dealership DMS platforms is not bound to the dealership that owns the record: a compromised account at one dealership can enumerate and retrieve customer records belonging to others on the same platform, so a single access-control failure is amplified across the entire shared customer base.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-1220: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: DMS data access is granted at role granularity rather than per transaction: sales and service staff accounts carry bulk export rights over the full customer database — purchase history, financing data and government identification — far exceeding what any individual deal requires, so one compromised staff credential exposes every customer the dealership has served.

components.name: Customer Financing and Credit Systems
components.description: Platforms processing vehicle financing applications containing credit scores, bank account details, employment data, and government identification — RouteOne, DealerSocket CRM, Dealertrack financing. These systems hold the highest-sensitivity financial data in the dealership ecosystem.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-311: Missing Encryption of Sensitive Data
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Unencrypted storage of customer financing records exposes credit scores, bank account details, Social Security numbers, and income verification data to any attacker who gains database access — the sensitivity of financing application data means a single unencrypted database represents a complete identity theft toolkit.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: SQL injection in financing system databases allows attackers to bypass application-layer access controls and extract bulk customer financial records — the consolidated nature of financing platforms means a single injection point yields credit data for every customer whose application was processed through the system.

threat: Commit Financial Fraud Against Automotive Dealerships
threat_description: Adversaries exploit authorization weaknesses, business logic flaws, and insider access in dealership financial systems to alter vehicle ownership records, approve fraudulent financing, manipulate payment transactions, and divert funds. Automotive dealerships process high-value transactions — a single vehicle sale involves financing approvals, trade-in valuations, payment processing, and title transfers, each representing a manipulation opportunity. The complexity of the dealership financial workflow, combined with the high value of individual transactions, creates a target environment where a single unauthorized modification can yield thousands to hundreds of thousands of dollars.

motives.motive: Manipulate vehicle financing records and ownership documentation for financial gain

components.name: Dealer Management System (DMS)
components.description: DMS platforms managing vehicle sales records, ownership transfers, and financial transaction histories — the authoritative system of record for all dealership financial activity and vehicle title management.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Authorization is not enforced on DMS financial write operations: insiders and compromised accounts can alter vehicle ownership records, sale prices, financing terms and trade-in valuations without a second approval, because the platform authorizes by role presence rather than by requiring dual control on high-value record modifications.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-472: External Control of Assumed-Immutable Web Parameter
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Financing and billing values that the DMS treats as immutable — quoted price, trade-in credit, down-payment terms, refund amount — are carried in client-controlled parameters and re-accepted on submission without server-side revalidation against the originating quote, so an attacker can create reservations with zero-payment terms, inflate trade-in credits, or trigger refund approvals through a sequence of individually legitimate-looking transactions.

components.name: Dealership Payment Systems
components.description: POS and payment processing infrastructure handling vehicle purchase payments, service transactions, and financial settlements — DealerSocket payment modules, integrated POS systems. These systems process the largest individual transactions in the retail automotive environment.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Authorization is not enforced on payment settlement and reversal operations: transaction identifiers can be manipulated to redirect settlements to attacker-controlled accounts, and high-value refunds and reversals are approved on a single account's authority rather than under dual control — the transaction values in automotive retail make each individual fraud event disproportionately costly.

threat: Sell Driver Behavioral and Location Data to Third Parties Without Consent
threat_description: Adversaries — including OEMs, data brokers, and third-party service providers — exploit the absence of meaningful consent mechanisms and data governance controls to monetize continuous driver location, behavioral, and vehicle performance data collected through connected vehicle telematics. Regulators in California, Oregon, and the EU launched enforcement actions in 2025 after investigations revealed OEMs selling precise geolocation data to insurance companies that used it to penalize drivers — without drivers' knowledge or meaningful consent. The harm is not a breach. The data was never stolen. It was collected lawfully, aggregated extensively, and sold to parties whose use of it was never disclosed.

motives.motive: Monetize continuous driver location and behavioral data through unauthorized third-party data sales

components.name: Vehicle Telematics Data Monetization Platform
components.description: OEM and third-party platforms aggregating and commercializing continuous vehicle telemetry — LexisNexis Risk Solutions, Verisk, OEM data monetization programs. These platforms sit between the raw telematics stream and the data buyers who purchase access to it.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Third-party data buyers are granted the same standing privilege over the raw telemetry stream that internal processing holds, rather than a reduced privilege scoped to aggregated or anonymized output — insurers, brokers and advertisers receive continuous location resolution that enables individual driver surveillance well beyond any disclosed use case, and nothing in the platform reduces that privilege at the point of sharing.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-1220: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Consent is captured and enforced as a single undifferentiated grant rather than per purpose, so the platform cannot restrict a third-party buyer's access to the uses a driver actually authorized — data collected for a safety or functional feature is served to insurers, brokers and advertisers under the same permission.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-359: Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Continuous precise geolocation data sold to insurance aggregators constitutes exposure of sensitive personal information — driver location histories reveal home addresses, medical facilities visited, religious institutions attended, and political associations, creating privacy harm far exceeding what drivers understood they were consenting to.
Data access and onward-sharing transactions are not recorded, so neither drivers nor regulators can reconstruct who accessed a location history, when, or for what purpose.

components.name: Connected Vehicle Consent Management System
components.description: The consent capture and management infrastructure through which drivers nominally authorize telematics data collection and sharing — in-vehicle setup flows, mobile app permissions, dealer-completed enrollment forms. Inadequate consent mechanisms are the root control failure enabling unauthorized data monetization.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-1220: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Consent is modelled as a single all-or-nothing grant with broad sharing pre-selected and opt-out buried in secondary settings, so drivers cannot separately authorize functional telematics, safety services and commercial data sharing. Accepting commercial monetization becomes a precondition for connected-vehicle features, and regulators determined that consent obtained this way is not valid authorization for those uses under CCPA and GDPR.

threat: Exploit Supplier Network Trust to Infiltrate OEM Manufacturing Systems
threat_description: Adversaries compromise small or mid-tier automotive suppliers — who hold trusted network access to OEM production systems but rarely have equivalent security controls — and use that access as a pivot point into OEM manufacturing infrastructure. Breaching a supplier opens a back door straight into an OEM's systems: the supplier's network access is real, the security is weaker, and the potential damage runs the entire supply chain. In 2025, the criminal group Qilin exploited this pattern to steal 500GB of engineering blueprints from a Japanese precision parts manufacturer, while separate incidents used supplier footholds to reach OEM production environments in Italy and Australia. The OEM perimeter is only as strong as the weakest supplier connection to it.

motives.motive: Use trusted supplier-to-OEM network connections to access and attack OEM production systems that are inaccessible from the internet

components.name: Automotive Supplier Network Integration
components.description: Network connections, EDI interfaces, and collaboration platforms linking Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers to OEM production and engineering environments — trusted paths established for legitimate supply chain integration that become lateral movement corridors when a supplier is compromised.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Supplier-held OEM integration credentials are stored without adequate protection and validated weakly at the OEM edge, so an attacker who compromises a supplier environment can harvest OEM-facing credentials and authenticate directly into OEM production networks — the connection is treated as legitimate because it presents valid credentials from a trusted supplier address range.

Supplier accounts and network connections hold privileges far beyond what their integration function requires, and OEM segmentation between supplier zones and production networks is insufficient to contain them — a parts logistics supplier able to reach OEM production scheduling hands an attacker production-disruption privilege the legitimate integration never needed.

components.name: OEM Supplier Collaboration Portal
components.description: Web-based portals providing suppliers with access to OEM engineering documents, production specifications, and scheduling systems — authenticated external-facing interfaces that bridge supplier and OEM environments.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: SSRF vulnerabilities in supplier collaboration portals allow attackers with portal access to pivot from the internet-facing supplier interface to internal OEM systems that are not directly accessible — using the portal's server-side network access to reach OEM production databases and engineering repositories.

Security-relevant events on supplier connections into OEM systems are not recorded, so lateral movement from a compromised supplier environment leaves no reconstructable trail — the traffic reads as ordinary supplier activity until its scope diverges detectably from normal behavior, and the omission prevents establishing which OEM systems were reached.

threat: Corrupt Vehicle-to-Everything Communications to Endanger Road Users
threat_description: Adversaries manipulate Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication infrastructure — including vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I), vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V), and vehicle-to-network (V2N) channels — to inject false messages that cause vehicles to make dangerous decisions based on fabricated road conditions. V2X systems are designed to prevent accidents by sharing real-time safety information: emergency vehicle proximity, traffic signal timing, road hazard warnings, and collision avoidance alerts. When these messages are spoofed, the safety system becomes the hazard. A falsified traffic signal phase causes vehicles to proceed into intersections against actual traffic. The attacker does not cause a crash directly — they cause the safety system to instruct vehicles to.

motives.motive: Inject false V2X messages to cause vehicles to make dangerous navigation decisions

components.name: V2X Communication Infrastructure
components.description: Roadside units (RSUs), V2X network controllers, and connected traffic management systems broadcasting safety-critical messages to equipped vehicles — DSRC and C-V2X infrastructure, smart intersection controllers, emergency vehicle notification systems.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-940: Improper Verification of Source of a Communication Channel
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: V2X receivers neither verify that a message originated from the roadside or vehicle unit it claims, nor check that its contents are physically plausible for that source: broadcasts are accepted on asserted identity alone, so a spoofed emergency-vehicle warning, false hazard alert or fabricated signal phase injected from an unauthorized transmitter is indistinguishable from genuine infrastructure traffic and causes vehicles to brake, yield or proceed into an intersection on fabricated road conditions.

Weak authentication on roadside V2X infrastructure management interfaces allows unauthorized modification of broadcast message parameters — an attacker who compromises a roadside unit can broadcast falsified safety messages to every vehicle in range continuously, creating persistent hazardous conditions at that location.

components.name: V2X Onboard Vehicle Processing Unit
components.description: Vehicle-side hardware and software processing received V2X messages and translating them into driver alerts or autonomous driving inputs — the onboard component that determines how the vehicle responds to received safety messages.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: V2X onboard processing units that accept unsigned firmware updates allow installation of modified message processing logic that accepts unauthenticated messages as valid — removing the vehicle's ability to detect spoofed V2X broadcasts from legitimate ones.

Failure to validate the geographic plausibility and source authenticity of received V2X messages allows attackers broadcasting from unauthorized locations to inject safety-critical alerts that the vehicle treats as originating from legitimate roadside infrastructure.

threat: Steal Vehicles Through Keyless Entry and In-Vehicle Network Access
threat_description: Adversaries defeat the radio and in-vehicle network controls that stand between a parked vehicle and a running one — relaying key fob transmissions, replaying rolling codes, and injecting messages directly onto the vehicle network through accessible wiring. The economics are unlike any other automotive attack: the tooling is inexpensive, openly traded, and needs no contact with the owner, the OEM cloud or any dealer system. A relay attack takes under a minute on the owner's driveway and leaves no forced-entry evidence. The same in-vehicle network access that starts the engine also reaches the body control, immobiliser and gateway functions the vehicle depends on to decide which commands are legitimate.

motives.motive: Steal a parked vehicle by defeating keyless entry

components.name: Passive Keyless Entry and Immobiliser Systems
components.description: Key fob and smart-key radio systems, rolling-code authentication, and the immobiliser that gates engine start — LF/UHF challenge-response links, UWB and BLE ranging in newer platforms, transponder-based immobiliser chips. These systems decide whether a key is present and genuine.

sub_components.name: Key fob signal capture and relay resistance

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: The keyless entry exchange authenticates a fob response without binding it to the physical distance or the time window of the challenge, so an adversary can capture a valid response and present it later, or relay a live challenge-response pair between the parked vehicle and a fob inside the owner's house. The vehicle cannot distinguish a relayed exchange from a fob standing beside it, and rolling-code counters do not help when the genuine response is forwarded rather than replayed.

The fob-to-vehicle radio link accepts an interposed party as an endpoint: two cheap relay units, one at the vehicle and one near the key, extend a link designed for a metre or two across an entire property, and nothing in the protocol requires the peer to prove it is the actual endpoint rather than a repeater. Distance bounding or UWB ranging is the control this weakness names as absent.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Engine start and immobiliser release are reachable as critical functions without an authentication step of their own: once a message asserting a valid key is present on the internal network, the powertrain acts on it, because the immobiliser check happens elsewhere and its result is trusted rather than re-verified at the point of use.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-1191: On-Chip Debug and Test Interface With Improper Access Control
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Debug and test interfaces on immobiliser and key-management controllers remain reachable in production silicon without access control, so an adversary with brief physical access can read the transponder secret or write a new key into the module directly, bypassing every radio-side control and producing a key the vehicle regards as factory-legitimate.

components.name: In-Vehicle Network and Body Control Modules
components.description: CAN, CAN-FD and automotive Ethernet segments carrying door, ignition, body and chassis messages, the body control module, and the central gateway that separates comfort from powertrain domains. Physically reachable at the headlight connector, wheel arch and under-dash harness on many platforms.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-940: Improper Verification of Source of a Communication Channel
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Vehicle network frames carry no source authentication: a CAN identifier asserts which function sent a message and receivers act on that assertion alone, so an adversary who reaches any segment can emit door-unlock, ignition and immobiliser frames that are byte-identical to genuine ones. Nothing downstream can attribute a frame to the module that legitimately owns that identifier.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Safety- and security-relevant vehicle network functions accept commands without any authentication step, because the bus protocols were specified for a closed physical network and have no identity primitive to enforce. Reaching the wiring is the whole of the access control.

sub_components.name: Body control module physical wiring access

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Vehicle network segments are physically reachable without opening the cabin: the headlight connector, wheel-arch harness and under-bumper wiring on many platforms expose a bus that carries body and ignition traffic, and no enclosure, tamper detection or physical barrier stands between an adversary and the network the vehicle trusts implicitly.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-1299: Missing Protection Mechanism for Alternate Hardware Interface
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Alternate hardware interfaces on the body control module — service connectors, unpopulated headers, and diagnostic pins intended for assembly-line use — carry no protection mechanism in production vehicles, so functions that were only ever meant to be reachable in a factory fixture stay reachable for the life of the vehicle.

motives.motive: Retain or obtain a working digital key to access a vehicle

components.name: Phone-as-Key and Digital Key Provisioning
components.description: Digital key issuance, sharing and revocation across the OEM account, the phone secure element and the vehicle — CCC Digital Key, Apple and Google wallet key provisioning, BLE and UWB proximity links. The binding between an account, a device and a vehicle is established and withdrawn here.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Digital key authentication accepts a spoofed device identity: the vehicle and the provisioning service establish trust from identifiers and signatures a device asserts about itself, and an adversary who can impersonate the paired handset at the BLE or UWB layer, or forge the attestation the service checks, obtains a key the vehicle treats as genuinely provisioned.

sub_components.name: Digital key provisioning and revocation lifecycle

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Authorization on digital key operations is not bound to current vehicle ownership: keys shared to other accounts survive a vehicle sale, trade-in or rental return because revocation depends on the vehicle being online to receive it and on the previous owner choosing to withdraw access, so a party with no present entitlement retains a working key.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-1220: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Shared digital keys are granted at a single coarse level rather than scoped to the operations the sharing actually intended — unlock, drive, boot access, telemetry and further re-sharing all travel together — so a key handed to a valet, a driver or a family member carries the full authority of the owner's own key.

threat: Compromise the Vehicle Cabin Through Infotainment and Cellular Interfaces
threat_description: Adversaries treat the infotainment head unit and the telematics control unit as the two doors into the vehicle that face outward continuously. Both run general-purpose operating systems, both parse untrusted input from Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, USB, cellular and broadcast radio, and both sit on internal networks shared with chassis and powertrain functions. A head unit that mounts a crafted USB filesystem or pairs with a spoofed handset is a code-execution target reachable without any account, credential or cloud access. Where the internal gateway does not constrain what these units may request, a cabin-side compromise becomes a vehicle-control compromise, and the vehicle's own position data can be falsified at the source rather than intercepted downstream.

motives.motive: Gain code execution on the infotainment head unit

components.name: In-Vehicle Infotainment and Head Unit
components.description: The cabin compute platform running navigation, media, phone projection and vehicle settings — Android Automotive, QNX and Linux head units, CarPlay and Android Auto projection, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi stacks, USB and SD media handling. The largest general-purpose software surface in the vehicle.

cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi pairing on the head unit authenticates weakly or not at all: fixed or absent PINs, just-works pairing accepted silently, and legacy profiles left enabled mean a nearby adversary can associate with the unit without the occupant approving anything, then reach media, phonebook and vehicle-settings services that assume any paired peer is the owner's device.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-1299: Missing Protection Mechanism for Alternate Hardware Interface
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: USB, SD and service ports on the head unit carry no protection mechanism against what is attached: the unit mounts arbitrary filesystems, parses metadata and media containers, and in many platforms will accept software from removable media, so a device left in a rental or shared vehicle reaches parsers running with substantial privilege.

Infotainment media, projection and navigation processes run with far more privilege than their function requires — frequently as a single privileged user with access to the vehicle network interface — so a defect in a media parser or a projection handler yields control of the whole unit rather than of one sandboxed component.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Head unit software passes externally influenced values — device names, media metadata, network identifiers, update paths — into shell invocations on the underlying Linux or Android platform without neutralisation, so a crafted Bluetooth device name or filename becomes command execution on the cabin compute platform.

motives.motive: Falsify the vehicle's position data

components.name: Telematics Control Unit and Cellular Interface
components.description: The always-connected cellular module bridging the vehicle to OEM cloud services, carrying eCall, remote command, OTA transport and GNSS positioning — the TCU SoC, its modem firmware, its SIM/eSIM identity and its interface onto the internal gateway. The vehicle's permanent internet-facing endpoint.

sub_components.name: Cellular interface exposure and internal segmentation

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-923: Improper Restriction of Communication Channel to Intended Endpoints
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: The telematics unit's communication channel is not restricted to its intended endpoints: the modem side accepts traffic from the carrier network and, in many designs, from the public internet, while the same unit holds an interface onto the internal vehicle gateway. Nothing constrains which peers may reach it or which internal destinations it may in turn address, so the cellular attack surface and the vehicle network are one hop apart.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-1256: Improper Restriction of Software Interfaces to Hardware Features
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: Software on the telematics SoC reaches hardware features — power and clock control, debug fabric, memory protection configuration — without the restrictions that would prevent it being used to induce faults, so an adversary with code execution on the application side can glitch the boundary that is supposed to separate modem, application and vehicle-network domains.

cwes.cwe_id: CWE-940: Improper Verification of Source of a Communication Channel
cwes.cwe_mapping_reason: The vehicle accepts GNSS as an unauthenticated broadcast and verifies nothing about its source: a low-power transmitter beside the vehicle overrides genuine satellite signals, and the position it dictates propagates into navigation, geofenced features, telematics reporting and usage-based insurance data as though it were measured. There is no plausibility check against odometry or inertial sensing to contradict it.
